Phakisa Freeway

By: Floris Kotze | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Tonight on Carte Blanche — the forgotten racetrack that once hosted MotoGP, and the racers fighting to bring it roaring back to life.

Unique Selling Point:
An emotional and visually striking insert about Phakisa Raceway — South Africa’s former MotoGP track — and the passionate locals leading its grassroots revival. From racers to mayors, this is a story of community pride, lost glory, and a second chance to put Welkom back on the map.

Summary:
Phakisa Raceway in Welkom was once the jewel of South African motorsport — a world-class circuit that hosted MotoGP and promised global attention. But years of neglect, red tape and shifting responsibility saw the track fall silent. Now, a determined group of riders, officials and community members are rallying to bring Phakisa back.

Through the eyes of racer and organiser Tobs Motlokoa, we revisit Phakisa’s rise and fall — and meet those pushing for a comeback. The Executive Mayor, local councillors, community voices and racers share their hopes for revival.

From rusted gates to renewed dreams, this is the fight to bring back South Africa’s great racing cathedral.

Further information:
• Shot on location in Welkom, Free State.
• Features interviews with the Executive Mayor of Matjhabeng, Phakisa’s current owners, Ward Councillor Estelle Dansey, local voice Lourius Erasmus, Tobs Motlokoa, and a competitive motorcycle racer.
• Presented by Xola Ntshinga
• Includes current site access
• Runtime: 10 minutes

Script:


(Xola) Tobs Molefe is a racer at heart…
Most weekends, you’ll find him on two wheels — at track days, bike meets, always pushing limits.
Racing means early mornings. He has to load his bike - then travel to the track.
But he can’t race here, in Welkom, even though one of the country’s best circuits is right on his doorstep.

(Xola) The gates are closed and the circuit, looks abandoned…

(Xola) Phakisa Freeway was once the home of MotoGP. I and many fans remember it well. Some of the world's best riders raced here and thousands of fans would gather to see them.

(Upsound MotoGP Commentary) The lights are on red….‘We're away! Who's made a good start? Rossi on the outside, Gibernau in the middle and Biaggi on the inside. Valentino Rossi in supreme form under the South African sunshine. Phakisa Freeway and it's at Welkom today.
Valentino Rossi wins the African Grand Prix for Yamaha…
Yeah, there could be a couple of castle lagers in the pump tonight for Jeremy Burgess and his crew.”

(Xola) MotoGP came to Phakisa in 1999 and stayed until 2004.
Big names came to Welkom and many here - still treasure those memories.

(Lourius) 250,000 people flocking to Welkom. People opening their houses with rooms for riders.

(Estelle) My father actually did a couple of races. And if you look back on the pictures, it's amazing to see what it was.

(Voxie Subtitle) Teams fought over accommodation. It was wonderful!

(Mayor) Our people were smiling during that period.

(Lourius) There was speed and sound. There was quarter mile races, air shows.

(Xola) But the track slowly fell into decline. Then, in 2023,
Motorsport South Africa, the country's motorsport body, suspended Phakisa's license. They said the track wasn't safe and hadn't been maintained. That means no official races can take place at the track. Major races were cancelled and tourism plans collapsed.

(Lourius) All those events, everything gone.

(Xola) We arrived in Welkom - looking to tell a story of hope — locals rallying to revive a once famous race track. But - it wasn’t long before we hit resistance… and realised, not everyone is as invested in Phakisa's revival.

(Woman Subtitle) We are getting the police. We are arresting you!
(Xola Subtitle) We did not jump over anything!
(Xola) That's a false allegation!

(Xola) It’s not just about the money. With no official races at Phakisa, it’s the young talent who end up paying the price. Lourius Erasmus raced here in his day. Now his son Arno, is trying to do the same.

(Xola) Do you think Phakisa not being there has taken that dream away from you?

(Arno) Definitely because sometimes we're not able to go to Joburg to practice. Then I start losing hope because I see other people practicing on the tracks I want to be on. In a way, it does throw the dream away.

(Lourius) It would have been much better if we had Phakisa.

(Xola) After years of neglect, the people of Welkom have had enough.
Local counsellors, former racers, everyday ordinary people are willing to work together to bring it back to life.

(Xola) We met with Ward Councillor Estelle Dansey, whose ward includes Phakisa.

(Estelle) We've got a lot of unemployed people here. And the first thing when anyone sees you is, do you have a job for me? Just simple things like cleaners for the tracks, security. You can create so many jobs just with that one white elephant standing there.

(Xola) But that's easier said than done. Phakisa is owned by the province's Gambling, Liquor and Tourism Authority.

According to the most recent publicly available report — for the 2023-24 financial year — the track’s total expenditure was just under R10.2 million.

Of that, R9.5 million went to ‘employee-related costs’ — including the salary of General Manager Refiloe Taku.
Phakisa also overspent by more than R600 000 in the same financial year.
Now while they claim to have stayed within budget for the current financial year, they couldn’t give us exact figures — those are still being finalised.
But with a crumbling racetrack and no official motoring events in years… where exactly is the money going?
The owners state, that, Phakisa is still operational and that it employs 28 officials — for administration, security, and general maintenance. The track continues to host corporate functions, advanced driving, drag racing, and other occasional events.
The land is owned by the Matjhabeng local Municipality. So the road ahead needs agreement from all sides.
We spoke to Executive Mayor Thanduxolo Khalipha, who believes there IS a way forward.

(Xola) Is this something that can be revived or sustained through local, municipal and national government?

(Mayor) Yes, we go on a 50-50 where you have private sector coming to the track and making sure that we are able also to invite public sector and then we can then run this track together.

(Xola) Looking at it in its current state is heartbreaking. It is devastating for any sport fans. There have been estimates made over a hundred million rand is sort of what we're looking at. Just to resurface the track itself would be anywhere in excess of R20 million.
And I think what makes it even more heartbreaking is that there are people who are willing to help fund the rebuild.
The difficulty as always is the politics.

(Xola) We saw the politics play out firsthand. While we were filming, security accused us of trespassing, even though the mayor had personally given us permission to be there.

(Xola) He gave us permission…. Mayor Khalipha.

(Security) But our manager said, because we see all the gates are closed, so they said no one was supposed to get inside.

(Xola) That's why we went to the mayor.

(Xola) Our explanation fell on deaf ears. But things took a strange turn when security phoned someone apparently higher up the chain... whose name was kept from us.

(Woman Subtitle) They have to get arrested. They can explain it in court. We will arrest them because they broke into our house. Without permission.

(Xola) The mayor made it very clear. That's the... Hello ma'am?

(Woman Subtitle) We don't know anything -
the Mayor did not speak to us about anything. He did not speak to anyone.

(Xola) That's fine. Would it be possible to get your name and number from the gentlemen?

(Woman Subtitle) You don't need my name! I don't know you, you don't know me.

(Security Subtitle) They jumped the fence here at the back.

(Xola Subtitle) We did not jump over anything!

(Xola)That's a false allegation. Okay? The gate was open. This is what I am saying… you can come with me.


(Xola Subtitle) The gate was like this.

(Xola) And there is no lock. And there is no sign. And then we got permission 3. And 4, the lady is making threats, but she doesn't want to give us a name. So maybe it's better… if the police come.

(Xola) The police arrived shortly afterwards. They explained they couldn't arrest us and that, if charges were to be laid, that would have to happen in person.

We later discovered the person who wanted us arrested was none other than Refiloe Taku, the general manager of Phakisa.
Taken aback by the hostility, we contacted her with our questions, but she referred us to the owners of the track, the Free State Gambling Liquor and Tourism Authority.
In a written response they denied that any of its officials — gave an instruction for anyone to be arrested.
Regarding the state of the facilities they confirmed that discussions are underway, to secure private investment for refurbishing and operating the racetrack.
(Tobs) Given the way Phakisa is, it is not the core function of government to run it like a business.

(Xola) Tobs, is not just a racer. He's part of a group of locals who want to work with government to bring Phakisa back and help run it in the future.

(Tobs) Currently, it's an entity that is sitting without generating any income and it's got massive potential. The best option is actually for government to give it to an entity that is going to run it like a business. At the same time, at least the government will be able to generate income. Let it go and let it be run effectively for the benefit of the province.

(Xola) Well the people here are very eager to see this place restored to its former glory. The name Phakisa, which means hurry up, in this instance seems very apt.

(Mayor) All of us speak with one voice. Phakisa must be revived.

(Lourius) I think we should act now. It's deteriorating every day. Three years down the line from now, it might not be revivable.

(Tobs) One of the reasons for the failures, I think, is simply because in government you don't have people who are passionate about motosport.
When the tough gets going, when you've got passion for it, then passion keeps you going.





PROMO 1

(Xola) Phakisa Raceway could still be the heartbeat of Welkom — if the right hands take the wheel.

(Mayor Khalipha) All of us speak with one voice. Phakisa must be revived.

(Xola) But the wait continues… and so does the decline.

PROMO 2

(Xola) For young riders in Welkom, the road to racing glory starts far from home.

(Arno Erasmus) If I don't have a track nearby, I can't practice and I'm starting to lose hope in a way.

(Xola) Without a track, this talent risks being left behind.

PROMO 3
(Xola) Tobs Molefe lives for motorsport. But at Phakisa — the gates are locked.

(Tobs) The dream can certainly be realized because I believe that in unity there is strength, in action there is victory.

(Xola) In Welkom, Victory means racing at Phakisa, just like before.

Of that, R9.5 million went to ‘employee-related costs’ — including the salary of General Manager Refiloe Taku. Phakisa also overspent by more than R600 000 in the same financial year. Now while they claim to have stayed within budget for the current financial year, they couldn’t give us exact figures — those are still being finalised. But with a crumbling racetrack and no official motoring events in years… where exactly is the money going? The owners state, that, Phakisa is still operational and that it employs 28 officials — for administration, security, and general maintenance. The track continues to host corporate functions, advanced driving, drag racing, and other occasional events. The land is owned by the Matjhabeng local Municipality. So the road ahead needs agreement from all sides. We spoke to Executive Mayor Thanduxolo Khalipha, who believes there IS a way forward. (Xola) Is this something that can be revived or sustained through local, municipal and national government? (Mayor) Yes, we go on a 50-50 where you have private sector coming to the track and making sure that we are able also to invite public sector and then we can then run this track together. (Xola) Looking at it in its current state is heartbreaking. It is devastating for any sport fans. There have been estimates made over a hundred million rand is sort of what we're looking at. Just to resurface the track itself would be anywhere in excess of R20 million. And I think what makes it even more heartbreaking is that there are people who are willing to help fund the rebuild. The difficulty as always is the politics. (Xola) We saw the politics play out firsthand. While we were filming, security accused us of trespassing, even though the mayor had personally given us permission to be there. (Xola) He gave us permission…. Mayor Khalipha. (Security) But our manager said, because we see all the gates are closed, so they said no one was supposed to get inside. (Xola) That's why we went to the mayor. (Xola) Our explanation fell on deaf ears. But things took a strange turn when security phoned someone apparently higher up the chain... whose name was kept from us. (Woman Subtitle) They have to get arrested. They can explain it in court. We will arrest them because they broke into our house. Without permission. (Xola) The mayor made it very clear. That's the... Hello ma'am? (Woman Subtitle) We don't know anything - the Mayor did not speak to us about anything. He did not speak to anyone. (Xola) That's fine. Would it be possible to get your name and number from the gentlemen? (Woman Subtitle) You don't need my name! I don't know you, you don't know me. (Security Subtitle) They jumped the fence here at the back. (Xola Subtitle) We did not jump over anything! (Xola)That's a false allegation. Okay? The gate was open. This is what I am saying… you can come with me. (Xola Subtitle) The gate was like this. (Xola) And there is no lock. And there is no sign. And then we got permission 3. And 4, the lady is making threats, but she doesn't want to give us a name. So maybe it's better… if the police come. (Xola) The police arrived shortly afterwards. They explained they couldn't arrest us and that, if charges were to be laid, that would have to happen in person. We later discovered the person who wanted us arrested was none other than Refiloe Taku, the general manager of Phakisa. Taken aback by the hostility, we contacted her with our questions, but she referred us to the owners of the track, the Free State Gambling Liquor and Tourism Authority. In a written response they denied that any of its officials — gave an instruction for anyone to be arrested. Regarding the state of the facilities they confirmed that discussions are underway, to secure private investment for refurbishing and operating the racetrack. (Tobs) Given the way Phakisa is, it is not the core function of government to run it like a business. (Xola) Tobs, is not just a racer. He's part of a group of locals who want to work with government to bring Phakisa back and help run it in the future. (Tobs) Currently, it's an entity that is sitting without generating any income and it's got massive potential. The best option is actually for government to give it to an entity that is going to run it like a business. At the same time, at least the government will be able to generate income. Let it go and let it be run effectively for the benefit of the province. (Xola) Well the people here are very eager to see this place restored to its former glory. The name Phakisa, which means hurry up, in this instance seems very apt. (Mayor) All of us speak with one voice. Phakisa must be revived. (Lourius) I think we should act now. It's deteriorating every day. Three years down the line from now, it might not be revivable. (Tobs) One of the reasons for the failures, I think, is simply because in government you don't have people who are passionate about motosport. When the tough gets going, when you've got passion for it, then passion keeps you going. PROMO 1 (Xola) Phakisa Raceway could still be the heartbeat of Welkom — if the right hands take the wheel. (Mayor Khalipha) All of us speak with one voice. Phakisa must be revived. (Xola) But the wait continues… and so does the decline. PROMO 2 (Xola) For young riders in Welkom, the road to racing glory starts far from home. (Arno Erasmus) If I don't have a track nearby, I can't practice and I'm starting to lose hope in a way. (Xola) Without a track, this talent risks being left behind. PROMO 3 (Xola) Tobs Molefe lives for motorsport. But at Phakisa — the gates are locked. (Tobs) The dream can certainly be realized because I believe that in unity there is strength, in action there is victory. (Xola) In Welkom, Victory means racing at Phakisa, just like before.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Tonight on Carte Blanche — the forgotten racetrack that once hosted MotoGP, and the racers fighting to bring it roaring back to life.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: An emotional and visually striking insert about Phakisa Raceway — South Africa’s former MotoGP track — and the passionate locals leading its grassroots revival. From racers to mayors, this is a story of community pride, lost glory, and a second chance to put Welkom back on the map.
metadata.Summary: Phakisa Raceway in Welkom was once the jewel of South African motorsport — a world-class circuit that hosted MotoGP and promised global attention. But years of neglect, red tape and shifting responsibility saw the track fall silent. Now, a determined group of riders, officials and community members are rallying to bring Phakisa back. Through the eyes of racer and organiser Tobs Motlokoa, we revisit Phakisa’s rise and fall — and meet those pushing for a comeback. The Executive Mayor, local councillors, community voices and racers share their hopes for revival. From rusted gates to renewed dreams, this is the fight to bring back South Africa’s great racing cathedral.
metadata.Further information: • Shot on location in Welkom, Free State. • Features interviews with the Executive Mayor of Matjhabeng, Phakisa’s current owners, Ward Councillor Estelle Dansey, local voice Lourius Erasmus, Tobs Motlokoa, and a competitive motorcycle racer. • Presented by Xola Ntshinga • Includes current site access • Runtime: 10 minutes
